name: Kargil
tagline: Purig's river town between Zoji La and Leh
meta_description: Kargil, Ladakh: the halfway town on the Srinagar–Leh road, Mulbekh's rock-cut Maitreya, Drass and the Suru valley to Zanskar. Costs, stays, routes.
summary: Kargil is Ladakh's second town, at 2,676 m on the Suru river, roughly halfway between Srinagar and Leh. Most people of the region are Shia Muslims who speak Purgi. Sleep here on the road trip from Srinagar, and use it as the start of the Suru valley road to Zanskar.
intro: Kargil is where most road travellers from Srinagar spend their first night in Ladakh, and most of them leave at dawn without looking around. That is a pity. The town sits in a bowl where the Suru river runs between bare brown slopes, with poplar and willow along the water and apricot orchards climbing the side valleys. The main bazaar sells dried apricots, copper and everyday goods to villages up and down the valley.

The old name for this country is Purig, and its people and language are still called Purgi. Most are Shia Muslims, and the mosques, the black flags of Muharram and the imambaras make Kargil feel quite different from Buddhist Leh. A few hours east, though, Mulbekh and Shergol are Buddhist villages with gompas on the cliffs, and the change between the two worlds happens over a few kilometres of road.

For planning, Kargil matters for two reasons. At 2,676 m it is a gentle first night for anyone driving from Srinagar over Zoji La, much kinder to the body than flying straight into Leh. And it is the gateway to the Suru valley, Rangdum, Pensi La and Zanskar, a long day's drive south past the white faces of Nun and Kun.

highlights.title: Mulbekh's rock-cut Maitreya
highlights.text: Forty kilometres east, a standing Maitreya about 9 m tall is carved into a rock pillar beside the highway at Mulbekh, with a small shrine built against it. Above the village, the Mulbekh gompa clings to a cliff. Stop for twenty minutes on the way to Lamayuru.

highlights.title: Kargil's main bazaar and apricots
highlights.text: Walk the main bazaar in the morning for dried apricots, apricot kernels and local copperware. In July and August fresh fruit arrives from the side valleys. Prices are lower than in Leh, and shopkeepers will tell you which village the fruit came from.

highlights.title: The Suru valley and Nun Kun
highlights.text: South of Kargil, the road follows the Suru river through Sankoo and Panikhar, with views of the Nun and Kun massif, both above 7,000 m. Even a half-day drive to Panikhar shows a greener, wetter Ladakh.

highlights.title: Drass and the memorial
highlights.text: Sixty kilometres west on the Srinagar road, Drass is often called one of the coldest inhabited places in Asia. The war memorial outside town honours soldiers who died in 1999, and most road travellers stop for a short visit.

highlights.title: Shergol's cliff gompa
highlights.text: Just east of Mulbekh, Shergol has a tiny white gompa set into a cliff face high above the Wakha river. It is a short, steep walk up from the road, best in morning light.

highlights.title: A gentle first night on the road
highlights.text: Coming from Srinagar, Kargil at 2,676 m is lower than Leh by more than 800 m. Sleeping here, then at Lamayuru or Alchi, is the easiest way to arrive in Ladakh without headaches.

field_notes.fact: Purig is the historical name of the Kargil region. Most of its people are Shia Muslims who speak Purgi, a Tibetic language closely related to Balti and Ladakhi.
The Mulbekh Chamba is a standing image of Maitreya, the future Buddha, about 9 m tall and carved in relief on a rock beside the Srinagar–Leh highway east of Kargil.
Drass, on the Srinagar road west of Kargil, sits at about 3,280 m and is often described as one of the coldest inhabited places in the world, with winter lows far below −20 °C.

how_to_reach.text: Most travellers fly to Leh or Srinagar and drive. Kargil's airstrip sees only occasional civil flights; check current status before you travel.

JKSRTC and Ladakh buses link Kargil with Leh and Srinagar in season, usually leaving early in the morning. Shared Sumo taxis also run from Srinagar and Leh. Timings and fares change; check current status before you travel.
From Srinagar ≈ 204 km · 6–7 h via Sonamarg, Zoji La and Drass. From Leh ≈ 220 km · 6–7 h via Lamayuru, Fotu La and Mulbekh. Zoji La usually opens in spring and closes with heavy snow in winter.

where_to_stay: Saver: the bazaar area has many simple hotels and guesthouses at ₹1,500–3,000 a double, popular with truckers and bus travellers. Comfort: a few established hotels along the Suru river and the main road offer heated rooms, attached bathrooms and restaurants at ₹3,500–7,000 a double. Signature: there is no luxury hotel in Kargil; we choose the best available hotel for one night and keep the money for the Nimmu or Leh end of the trip.
tips: Kargil is conservative: dress modestly, and avoid public displays of affection.
During Muharram, processions fill the bazaar; plan around them and do not photograph mourners without asking.
Leave early for Leh or Srinagar to cross Fotu La or Zoji La before afternoon traffic.
Withdraw cash here if you are heading to Zanskar; Padum's ATM is not always reliable.
Buy dried apricots in Kargil's bazaar; they are often cheaper than in Leh.

experiences.title: Mulbekh's Maitreya and the Shergol cliff gompa
experiences.summary: Drive east from Kargil into Buddhist Purig to see the 9 m rock-cut Maitreya at Mulbekh, the cliff-top Mulbekh gompa and the small cave gompa at Shergol, three stops within 10 km of each other.
body: Forty kilometres east of Kargil, the highway leaves Muslim villages behind and enters Buddhist country. At Mulbekh a tall rock stands beside the road, and carved into its face is a standing Maitreya about 9 m tall, the future Buddha, with a small shrine built in front. Prayer flags run from the rock to the poplars.

Above the village, the Mulbekh gompa sits on a sheer cliff. A narrow road and a steep walk lead up; ask in the village if a monk can open the shrines. A few kilometres further east, Shergol's small white gompa is set into a cliff face above the Wakha river, a stiff 20-minute climb from the road.
Combine all three as a morning trip from Kargil, or as stops on the drive to Lamayuru and Leh. Walk around shrines clockwise, remove shoes inside, and leave a small donation.

faqs.q: How old is the Mulbekh Maitreya?
faqs.a: The carving is generally dated to well over a thousand years ago, from the period before Tibetan Buddhism spread widely in Ladakh, though scholars give different dates. It is one of the oldest Buddhist images on the Srinagar–Leh road. A small temple has been built against its base.

faqs.q: How far is Mulbekh from Kargil?
faqs.a: Mulbekh is about 40 km east of Kargil on the Srinagar–Leh highway, roughly an hour's drive. Shergol is a few kilometres further. Both are directly on the route to Lamayuru and Leh, so most travellers stop on the way rather than making a separate trip.

Yes. The rock-cut Maitreya is right beside the road with no climb. The gompas at Mulbekh and Shergol involve steep paths, so seniors may prefer to view them from below. The altitude here, around 3,300 m, is moderate.

experiences.title: The Suru valley to Panikhar and Nun Kun
experiences.summary: Follow the Suru river south from Kargil past Sankoo to Panikhar, where meadows and willow groves face the snow and ice of the Nun Kun massif. It is the first stage of the road to Zanskar and makes a good day out on its own.
body: The Suru valley is Ladakh's wetter, greener side. From Kargil the road runs south along the river through fields of barley and peas, past Sankoo with its willow groves and side valleys, to Panikhar, about 65 km from town. Villages here are mostly Shia, with small mosques and imambaras.

Beyond Panikhar, the valley opens and the white peaks of Nun and Kun, both above 7,000 m, appear above the glaciers. Walk along the fields, eat a packed lunch by the river, and turn back in the early afternoon. If you are travelling to Zanskar, this is the first half of the day's drive to Rangdum.
The road is paved in parts and rough in others, and landslides can close sections after rain. Carry snacks, water and warm layers, and go with a local driver who knows the valley.

faqs.q: How far is Panikhar from Kargil?
faqs.a: Panikhar is about 65 km south of Kargil up the Suru valley, roughly 2.5–3 hours by road depending on conditions. A taxi day trip costs about ₹4,500–6,000 for the car. The road continues to Parkachik, Rangdum and Pensi La on the way to Zanskar.

faqs.q: Can I see Nun and Kun from the road?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear days. The massif comes into view beyond Panikhar and is closest around Parkachik, where a glacier reaches down towards the river. Mornings are usually clearest; clouds often build by afternoon in July and August.

faqs.q: Is the Suru valley safe to visit?
faqs.a: Yes. It is a farming valley used by travellers heading to Zanskar, and villagers are used to visitors. Dress modestly, ask before photographing people, and follow your driver's advice on road conditions after rain. Check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Drass and the war memorial on the Srinagar road
experiences.summary: Drass, 60 km west of Kargil, is a high village known for hard winters. The war memorial beside the road remembers soldiers who died in 1999. Most road travellers stop here between Zoji La and Kargil.
body: Drass lies in a broad valley at about 3,280 m, between Zoji La and Kargil, and is often described as one of the coldest inhabited places in the world. In summer it is green, with meadows and sheep along the river, and the village is a natural stop for tea on the long drive from Srinagar.

Just outside town, the war memorial is a sandstone and lawn complex with a museum room and a wall of names. Visitors walk around quietly; it is a place of remembrance for families and soldiers, not a sightseeing spot. Allow 45 minutes.
If you are driving from Srinagar, plan the stop on the way to Kargil. From Kargil it is a half-day return trip. Follow all army instructions and photography signs.

faqs.q: How far is Drass from Kargil?
faqs.a: Drass is about 60 km west of Kargil on the Srinagar–Leh highway, roughly 1.5–2 hours by road. From Srinagar it is about 145 km via Sonamarg and Zoji La. Shared taxis and buses on the Srinagar–Kargil route pass through it.

faqs.q: Is Drass really the coldest place in India?
faqs.a: Drass is often described as one of the coldest inhabited places in the world, with winter lows far below −20 °C and heavy snow. In summer, days are mild at 15–25 °C. If you travel in May or October, carry warm layers for evenings.

faqs.q: Is photography allowed at the war memorial?
faqs.a: Photography of the memorial grounds is generally allowed, but some areas and any military installations nearby are not to be photographed. Read the signs, follow staff instructions, and behave quietly as you would at any memorial.

faqs.q: Is Kargil worth visiting or just a night halt?
faqs.a: Most travellers use Kargil as a night halt between Srinagar and Leh, but it rewards an extra half day. Walk the bazaar for apricots, drive to Mulbekh's rock-cut Maitreya, or follow the Suru valley towards Nun Kun. If you are heading to Zanskar, Kargil is the natural base.

faqs.q: How far is Kargil from Leh and Srinagar?
faqs.a: Kargil is about 220 km from Leh, 6–7 hours via Lamayuru and Fotu La, and about 204 km from Srinagar, 6–7 hours via Zoji La and Drass. Buses and shared taxis run both ways in season, usually leaving early in the morning.

Yes. Kargil is a working town that sees many travellers on the Srinagar–Leh road. It is conservative, so dress modestly, keep public behaviour low-key and ask before photographing people. During Muharram there are large religious processions; travel around them respectfully.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Kargil?
faqs.a: No permit is needed for Kargil town, Drass, Mulbekh, the Suru valley or Zanskar. Carry photo ID for routine checkposts. Some areas near the Line of Control are restricted; follow army instructions. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Kargil?
faqs.a: Kargil town is about 2,676 m, much lower than Leh. That makes it the gentlest first night for anyone driving into Ladakh from Srinagar. Drass, west of town, is higher at about 3,280 m, and Fotu La on the way to Leh reaches 4,108 m.

Zoji La, between Sonamarg and Drass, usually opens to traffic in spring and closes after heavy snow in winter, with exact dates set by road authorities each year. A tunnel is under construction. Check current status before you travel and leave early, as the pass can be one-way at times.

faqs.q: Is there an ATM and mobile network in Kargil?
faqs.a: Yes. Kargil has several bank ATMs in the main bazaar. Postpaid connections from major networks work in town; prepaid SIMs from outside Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh usually do not. Coverage fades quickly in the Suru valley and towards Zanskar.

faqs.q: What food should I try in Kargil?
faqs.a: Try local bread from the bazaar bakeries, mutton dishes and apricot in every form: dried fruit, kernels and the apricot-kernel oil used in cooking. Many hotels serve Kashmiri and north Indian food. Kargil is mostly a non-alcoholic town, so do not expect bars.

faqs.q: Can I go from Kargil to Zanskar in one day?
faqs.a: It is possible but very long: Kargil to Padum is about 235 km over Pensi La, 10–12 hours of rough driving. We prefer breaking the journey at Rangdum, about 130 km from Kargil, especially for families and older travellers. Check road status before you travel.
